6203.stem:
Farmer Ellis wishes to use the region for livestock. Knowing that he can fit 12 sheep per hectare (10,000$\text{m}^2$), he figures that he can fit a flock of 660 sheep. He didn't have Six Maps to calculate the area, so he used the method and working out shown below:

\exfigure{3307_q3_1}

figures.cap: Triangle with sides a, b, c and Farmer Ellis's handwritten working
Triangle with blanks for angles A, B, C and sides a, b, c

parts.latex: Explain why Farmer Ellis is most likely incorrect with his area calculation:
Using the cosine rule and your measured side lengths on the previous page, find the size of the angle opposite side c in the triangle, rounding your answer to the nearest minute.
Calculate the area of the field. Round to the nearest 100$\text{m}^2$.

Using the sine rule for at least one angle, calculate the other two angles in the triangle to the nearest minute. As such, complete the triangle below.

\exfigure{3307_q3_2}

solutions.latex:
Farmer Ellis has assumed the paddock has a right angle and has used side $c$ as the height, which is the wrong formula.

He should have used

$$A = \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$$

Using the cosine rule for the angle opposite side $c$:

$$\begin{aligned} \cos C &= \dfrac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab} \\ &= \dfrac{1290^2 + 1260^2 - 880^2}{2 \times 1290 \times 1260} \\ &= 0.762\ldots \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} C &= \cos^{-1}(0.762\ldots) \\ &= 40^\circ 21' \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the area formula with the included angle $C$:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1290 \times 1260 \times \sin(40^\circ 21') \\ &\approx 526\,200 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct substitution into the area formula, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; rubric written by us (2 marks per the question).

solutions.latex:
Using the sine rule:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin B}{1260} &= \dfrac{\sin 40^\circ 21'}{880} \\ B &= \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sin 40^\circ 21'}{880} \times 1260\right) \\ &= 67^\circ 59' \end{aligned}$$

Using the angle sum of a triangle:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= 180^\circ - 67^\circ 59' - 40^\circ 21' \\ &= 71^\circ 40' \end{aligned}$$

The completed triangle has

$$\begin{aligned} A &= 71^\circ 40' & a &= 1290 \text{ m} \\ B &= 67^\circ 59' & b &= 1260 \text{ m} \\ C &= 40^\circ 21' & c &= 880 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one angle using the sine rule, or equivalent merit
Uses the sine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source's $B$ value appears slightly off if sine rule is used with side b over sin B (sin B = 1260 sin C / 880 gives about 111 or 69 degrees); kept as source.

3307_q3_1.notes: Drew the triangle with the vertices measured from the crop: thin 0.6pt lines (rule 3), labels a, b, c in maths italic at the crop's positions and clear of the sides (rules 11, 19). Farmer Ellis's working is in a plain rectangle at the same position: same lines, line breaks and alignment, fractions stacked (rule 23). The crop's wavy paper edge, the handwriting font and the scan's heavy triangle stroke are not copied (rules 3, 10, 19), and the working is typeset in the house font. The low overlay scores come only from the handwriting font versus typeset glyphs and the wavy border; the triangle and labels line up exactly.

3307_q3_2.notes: Triangle with six answer blanks ('Angle B:', 'Side c:' etc.) placed where the crop has them; text set flush right to each blank line. Letters are in maths italic (rule 19). Lines are 0.6pt (rules 1, 2, 3). The leftover overlay difference comes from the scan's thicker strokes and its sans-serif font.

6328.stem:
Geoffrey is planning a bushwalk. He plans to start from his house in Kenthurst ($K$) and walk to Glenhaven ($G$) which is 5 km away at a bearing of $160^\circ\text{T}$. Geoffrey is then planning to walk to Rouse Hill ($R$) which is 4 km from Glenhaven at a bearing of $\text{N}50^\circ\text{E}$.

\exfigure{716_q21_1}

figures.cap: bushwalk diagram with points K, G, R and north arrows
solution sketch: diagram labelled with 160 degrees, 5 km, 50 degrees, 4 km

parts.latex: Label the above diagram with the given information.
Geoffrey plans to return to his home in Kenthurst directly from Rouse Hill. Calculate the distance of this trip, correct to 2 decimal places
Find the true bearing of Kenthurst from Rouse Hill.

solutions.latex:
The angle between $GK$ and north at $G$ is found from co-interior angles, which add to $180^\circ$:
$$180^\circ - 160^\circ = 20^\circ$$
The bearing of $R$ from $G$ is $\text{N}50^\circ\text{E}$, so
$$\angle KGR = 20^\circ + 50^\circ = 70^\circ$$
as required.

Let $KR = x$. By the cosine rule in triangle $KGR$:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 &= 4^2+5^2-2\times 4\times 5\times\cos 70^\circ \\ &= 27.319\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x \approx 5.23 \text{ km (2 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Substitutes correctly into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $\theta = \angle GRK$, the angle at $R$ between $RG$ and $RK$. By the sine rule in triangle $KGR$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{5} = \dfrac{\sin 70^\circ}{5.23}$$
$$\sin\theta = \dfrac{5\sin 70^\circ}{5.23}$$
$$\theta \approx 64.01^\circ$$
The bearing of $G$ from $R$ is $180^\circ + 50^\circ = 230^\circ\text{T}$, and $K$ lies further round, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 230^\circ + 64^\circ \\ &= 294^\circ\text{T} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the sine rule with correct substitution, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source wrote $\angle HRG$; changed to $\angle GRK$ to match the described angle at $R$. Rubric written by us.

716_q21_1.notes: Bearing diagram K–G–R with filled north arrows and bold italic point labels, as in the crop. Rules 1, 4.

716_q21_s1.notes: Same layout as the question figure, plus true arcs for the 160° bearing at K (north clockwise to KG) and the 50° angle at G (north to GR), and the labels 5 km and 4 km beside their sides, typeset in place of the handwriting (rule 17). The original-side score is low only because of the handwritten blue ink.

6615.stem: Two hikers decide to leave a campsite ($C$) to visit some natural landmarks in the area. One hiker walks 16 km on a bearing of $65^\circ$ to see a lake ($L$); the other hiker walks 26 km on a bearing of $285^\circ$ to reach the top of a mountain ($M$).

figures.cap: incomplete diagram: campsite with north line and two unlabelled endpoints
solution sketch: hand-completed diagram with bearings, lengths and angle theta

parts.latex:
Complete the diagram to display the scenario. Include lengths and bearings from the question above.

\exfigure{823_q19_1}
Calculate the distance between the mountain and the lake, correct to the nearest kilometre.
Hence, using your answer from part b) and the sine rule, find the bearing of the lake from the mountain, correct to the nearest degree.

solutions.latex:
In triangle $CLM$, $\angle LCM=140^\circ$ (the bearings $65^\circ$ and $285^\circ$ differ by $220^\circ$, so the angle on the other side is $360^\circ-220^\circ=140^\circ$). Using the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} c^2 &= 26^2+16^2-2\times 26\times 16\times\cos 140^\circ \\ &= 1569.34\ldots \\ c &= 39.615\ldots \\ &\approx 40 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes correctly into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Explanation of the $140^\circ$ angle added.

solutions.latex:
Let $\theta=\angle CML$. Using the sine rule in triangle $CLM$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\theta}{16} &= \dfrac{\sin 140^\circ}{40} \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{16\sin 140^\circ}{40} \\ \theta &= 14.89\ldots^\circ \end{aligned}$$
The bearing of the lake from the mountain is
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 180^\circ-75^\circ-\theta \\ &\approx 90^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing is } 090^\circ$$
criteria: Substitutes correctly into the sine rule

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. The step $180^\circ-75^\circ-\theta$ is kept from the source without further explanation.

No labels added because the student completes the diagram. The crop's heavy strokes and large arrowheads are drawn at house weight 0.6pt with standard Latex heads (rules 3 and 4).
